title: Dynamic affinity kernel orchestration for paged-KV + fused FlashAttention notes
content:
Summary:

This doc collects notes and an early sketch for a runtime-level kernel orchestration layer that uses soft affinity hints to steer CUDA kernel placement and launch ordering for paged-KV workloads with fused FlashAttention-like kernels. Goal: reduce p95/p99 tail latency and variance without hurting overall throughput or increasing memory pressure significantly.

Key idea (one-liner):
Give per-request and per-token affinity hints to the scheduler (based on KV residency, token age, and priority tier) and use those to:
- pick kernel launch streams and priorities
- bundle compatible kernels to reduce SM-waste and kernel-launch overhead
- prefer prewarmed/fused kernels when local KV pages are resident
- fall back to lower-cost non-fused kernels when contention/eviction is likely

Why we need this:
- Paged-KV introduces high variance: some requests are hot (most KV in GPU), others require page loads.
- FlashAttention-fused kernels are fast when KV and activations fit in the right locality; but their latency is sensitive to prefetch timing and SM occupancy.
- Current naive FIFO/priority queueing at the stream level can't express the affinity between a kernel and a KV slab/resident page set.

Design goals and constraints:
- Primary objective: minimize tail latency (p95/p99) for realtime SLOs (e.g., 50 ms p95 target for short-context use cases).
- Secondary objective: maintain or improve aggregate throughput (tokens/sec) and GPU utilization.
- No change to model weights or user-visible API semantics. Hints derive from scheduler and telemetry.
- Keep complexity manageable; prefer heuristic-driven policies over heavy-weight ML-based schedulers for initial rollout.

Affinity signals we can use:
- KV residency score: fraction of pages for the request already resident in GPU memory (0..1).
- Token age: number of tokens already generated in session; newer tokens often reuse recent KV state so higher locality.
- Request priority tier: e.g., latency-sensitive vs batch/async.
- Model variant compatibility: fused FlashA kernel available for this model & quantization; kernel supports current sequence length.
- Memory slab affinity: which KV slab(s) the request will touch (slab id strings).

Runtime components sketch:
1) Affinity annotator (per-request): produces a small affinity vector { residency:0.0-1.0, slab_id: <id>, priority: L/M/H, token_age:int }. Runs in control-plane path before scheduling.
2) Launch planner: consumes affinity vectors and decides kernel launch grouping and stream assignment. Heuristics:
   - High-residency & H-priority -> fast-path: launch on high-priority CUDA stream, prefer fused kernel variant, preemptible bundling with other high-residency kernels up to occupancy budget.
   - Low-residency -> defer kernel until prefetch completes (if prefetch scheduled) OR schedule on lower-priority stream to avoid disturbing high-priority fast-paths.
   - Same slab_id & same model variant -> co-locate kernels within same stream group to leverage slab-locality and reduce competing DMA.
3) Stream groups and priorities: maintain a handful of logical stream groups: realtime-high (priority), realtime-low, background-batch. Implement via CUDA stream priorities + per-SM occupancy caps (via kernel launch grid sizing heuristics).
4) Bundle manager: merges small kernels from compatible requests into a single batched launch when doing so reduces per-token latency without increasing queuing delay. Bundles are conservative: only merge when per-request waiting time < threshold and total batch size < batch_ceiling_for_latency.
5) Fallback and preempt: if a high-priority kernel gets stuck waiting for DMA page-in beyond SLO budget, launch fallback non-fused kernel variant that can make progress with partial KV (approximate) or route to CPU-fallback.

Kernel placement heuristics (practical rules):
- If residency > 0.8 and token_age < 32 -> fused FlashA on high-prio stream.
- If residency between 0.3 and 0.8 -> attempt to prefetch pages (async DMA) and schedule kernel on low-prio stream to avoid blocking high-prio. If prefetch completes within prefetch_timeout -> promote to high-prio fused run.
- If residency < 0.3 -> do not use fused kernel; use streaming-friendly kernel that tolerates missing KV pages and performs incremental page pulls.

Microbenchmark plan (what to measure):
- Latency distribution (p50/p90/p95/p99) for synthetic mixes: 80/20 hot/cold, 50/50, and all-cold; measure with/without affinity orchestration enabled.
- Throughput (tokens/sec) at multiple concurrency levels (1-128 concurrent requests).
- GPU utilization drift and DMA saturation.
- Cost of bundling: quantify extra queuing delay introduced vs RPC-level latency saved.
- Eviction interaction: measure number of page thrashing events and extra page loads caused by co-location heuristics.

Initial experiments we ran (summary):
- Simple prototype: attach residency score (0/1) and two stream priorities. Observed p95 improvements of ~12% on 80/20 workload, but small throughput decrease (~4%) at high concurrency due to underutilized SMs caused by strict segregation.
- Bundling naive test: merging two high-residency requests into one batched kernel reduced per-request overhead (launch latency) but increased p99 slightly when one request had longer pre-existing KV wait. Need smarter hold-time thresholding.

Open implementation details / engineering notes:
- Tracking slab_id: we need a compact representation that can be used as a map key for co-location decisions. Use 16-bit slab hashes derived from global KV index; collisions rare and ok for heuristics.
- Interaction with current prefetcher: the launch planner must be able to query prefetch status and optionally trigger higher-priority prefetch for H-priority requests. This requires coordination with page-manager API.
- CUDA stream creation: prefer reusing a small fixed pool of streams per device with different priorities. Avoid creating streams per request.
- Kernel fusion registry: runtime must know kernel variants available (fused_flashattn_vX, fallback_streaming_vY) and constraints (max_seq_len, quantization support). Expose a small JSON manifest for each model.
- Safety: ensure fallbacks preserve correctness (numerical differences allowed only if within eval thresholds).

Edge cases and failure modes:
- Thrashing: aggressive co-location of slabs can increase DMA contention; need to track DMA queue depth and backoff.
- Starvation: if high-priority stream is overloaded, low-priority kernels might never run; set global fairness counters and spillover windows.
- Fragmented bundles: merging kernels across requests with mismatch in runtime can create stragglers; only bundle similar estimated-cost kernels.

Telemetry and observability needs:
- Per-request affinity vector logs ( residency, slab_id, chosen_stream, chosen_kernel_variant, prefetch_action ).
- Metrics: p50/p90/p95/p99 by residency bucket; DMA bandwidth by slab; bundle success rate; fallback rate.
- Dashboards: add a per-model panel showing kernel_variant distribution and tail-latency correlation with residency.

Rollout plan:
- Phase 0: telemetry-only. Emit affinity vectors and offline analysis for two weeks.
- Phase 1: conservative runtime with only H-priority fast-path (no bundling). Evaluate p95 improvements.
- Phase 2: enable bundling for high-residency short-token requests with strict hold-time thresholds. Monitor p99.
- Phase 3: enable promotion/demotion and adaptive prefetching.

Open research / next steps (nice-to-have):
- ML-based admission controller: predict whether a fused run will finish before SLO using lightweight models on affinity + current DMA queues.
- Per-SM occupancy shaping via CUDA-occupancy APIs or kernel grid sizing that dynamically reduces threadblocks for latency-sensitive kernels to reserve SMs.
- Hardware-aware slab placement: place frequently co-accessed slabs on same physical memory region to reduce DMA scatter.

Concrete TODOs (short-term):
- [ ] Add slab_id to page-manager API and emit residency metric (Samir)
- [ ] Implement small affinity annotator in control-plane and wire into planner proto (Elena)
- [ ] Create kernel-manifest format and add entries for current fused/non-fused variants (Priya)
- [ ] Run synthetic microbenchmarks for 80/20 and 50/50 mixes and record p95/p99 (Jon)
- [ ] Design dashboard prototype for residency-bucket tail-latency (Elena)

Questions for the group:
- What should the residency thresholds be in practice? Start with 0.8/0.3 and iterate?
- Are we comfortable with a conservative fallback that sacrifices some quality for latency on H-tier requests? Do we need an explicit quality-cutoff per customer?
- How to surface affinity tuning knobs in Console without overwhelming customers? (Default auto, advanced manual knobs?)

Notes to self / scribbles:
- affinity vector should be as small as possible (3-4 bytes) when transported in RPC headers. Could pack residency into one byte, slab_id 2 bytes, priority 1 byte.
- consider a per-device lightweight admission token bucket for high-prio fused kernels to enforce fairness across tenants.

Appendix: tiny pseudocode sketch (planner heuristic)

// pseudo description, not runnable code
for each incoming request r:
  v = annotator(r) // residency, slab_id, priority, token_age
  if v.priority == H and v.residency > 0.8 and kernel_manifest.has_fused(r.model):
    assign_stream(r, HIGH_PRIO)
    choose_kernel_variant(r, fused)
  else if v.residency < 0.3:
    assign_stream(r, LOW_PRIO)
    choose_kernel_variant(r, streaming_fallback)
  else:
    if prefetch_manager.is_prefetching(v.slab_id):
      assign_stream(r, LOW_PRIO)
    else:
      trigger_prefetch(v.slab_id, urgency_by_priority(v.priority))
      assign_stream(r, LOW_PRIO)

End of doc.

-- Elena
